name: Ellagic acid

lead: Ellagic acid is a polyphenol found in pomegranates, berries and walnuts, used in supplements and in some skin-care products as an antioxidant and brightener for a fresher, more even complexion.

In laboratory assays it scavenges free radicals, which is the basis for the antioxidant claim. When eaten, gut bacteria convert it into urolithins, which are absorbed better than the parent compound, and much of the research concerns these metabolites. No trial of its brightening effect on skin was found.

paras: It is used as a topical ingredient in brightening products and as an oral supplement or through foods such as pomegranate and berries.
Wikipedia reports the FDA has issued warning letters to supplement companies over disease claims. No safety profile was found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Used in brightening products and supplements as an antioxidant, aiming for less dullness and a brighter complexion. It scavenges free radicals in lab assays. No skin trials of the brightening use were found.

lead: Ellagic acid is a naturally occurring polyphenol, the dilactone of hexahydroxydiphenic acid, found in foods such as pomegranates, raspberries, strawberries, walnuts and grapes, where it is released from ellagitannins [1][2]. It is marketed as an antioxidant and, in some skin-care products, as a brightening ingredient.

Most research concerns its antioxidant activity and its gut-microbiota metabolites, the urolithins [3][4][5]. The sources reviewed contain no clinical trial of ellagic acid for skin brightening. Wikipedia reports that it is sold as a supplement with claims against cancer and other diseases, that there is no scientific evidence for such claims, and that the FDA has issued warning letters over such claims [2].
infobox: Low as free compound; metabolized by gut bacteria to urolithins

paras: Ellagic acid is formed by hydrolysis of ellagitannins and is described as poorly soluble in water [1][2]. Wikipedia lists chestnuts, walnuts, pecans, cranberries, raspberries, strawberries and grapes among foods containing it, with pomegranate juice a rich source [2]. Studies of pomegranate juice attribute much of its antioxidant activity to its phenolic composition, including punicalagin and ellagic acid [3][4].

Wikipedia reports that about 90% of ellagic acid is unabsorbed in the intestine until gut microflora metabolize it into urolithins, which are more bioavailable [2]. The biological significance of these metabolites, and the role of gut microbiota in polyphenol bioavailability, have been reviewed [5][6].

In vitro work reported antiproliferative, apoptotic and antioxidant activity of pomegranate polyphenols including ellagic acid, enhanced in combination with other polyphenols [4]. Reviews place polyphenols among dietary agents studied for cancer prevention, largely in preclinical settings [7][8]. Grokipedia notes that human clinical evidence for cancer and other conditions remains limited and preliminary [1].

No studies found on skin brightening or appearance use. Registered human trials involving ellagic acid or ellagitannin-rich foods address other outcomes: a trial in healthy men comparing ellagic acid from pomegranate juice with pure ellagic acid, a trial of a supplement for immune response to HPV infection, a phase 2 trial on metabolic syndrome components, and, in a further registered study, pharmacokinetics of pomegranate phenolics and urolithins [9][10][11]. A registered trial compared strawberry extract with hydrogen peroxide for tooth staining [12].
